audience_one_line: Someone who has seen a company announce a 'buyback' and wants to understand what it actually is — the mirror image of an IPO — how a company buys its own shares back, the two methods, and the limits SEBI puts on it.
must_answer: What a buyback is in plain terms: a company using its own cash to buy back its own shares from shareholders, then cancelling them — the reverse of raising money by issuing shares. It returns capital instead of raising it, and shrinks the share count.

The two methods: a tender offer (the company offers to buy back from existing holders on a proportionate basis through a letter of offer) and the open-market route (buying on the stock exchange, subject to sub-limits).
The headline limit: a buyback cannot exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves.
Where the money can come from: free reserves, the securities premium account, or the proceeds of a share issue — but not the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares.
The debt guardrail: after the buyback, the company's debt cannot exceed twice its paid-up capital and free reserves (a 2:1 ratio).

What happens to the shares: they must be fully paid-up to be bought back, and the company must extinguish and physically destroy them within seven working days of the buyback period ending — the share capital is genuinely reduced. A company cannot buy its own shares back through a subsidiary or investment company.
must_not_say: Investment advice — whether a buyback is bullish, whether to tender, how it affects the share price for an investor.
Tax treatment of buyback proceeds (not in the corpus).
Empirical/market-practice claims ('companies usually buy back when…') not in the source.
Specific open-market sub-limit percentages unless clearly grounded; the source describes a phased reduction without a single clean current number, so describe it qualitatively.
Any figure or rule not in the excerpts.
angle: Frame the buyback as the mirror image of an IPO — a company returning capital by buying and cancelling its own shares, rather than raising it by issuing them. Lead with that plain idea, then ground the mechanics (tender vs open market), the 25% cap, the funding sources, the 2:1 debt guardrail, and the mandatory extinguishment that makes the capital reduction real. Pairs with the primary-issue-family piece, which names the buyback as the route it leaves off its map.
